questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Preceding all else, a bit of catharsis: Do not(!!!) attend USYD on exchange if you are a MSc Statistics, or a MSc Mathematics student wanting to take masters-level (‘post graduate in USYD-lingo) statistics, data science, biostatistics or mathematics courses, because you will not be able to.
They have no course combination of four courses (units in USYD-lingo) within these areas available for you to choose from, no matter what the course website says!
Your only option is to either mix undergraduate units in, take non-statistics/non-mathematics units, take the CBS-style QBUS units, or spam (via mail, via phone, carrier-pigeons, …) lecturers and administrators (at institutes, at faculties, for the course, …) for months(!) to argue that you are able to take machine learning courses even though you do not have a Computer Science background.
Advisory warning current as of academic year 2024. For a true list of courses offered to exchange students (as opposed to the ones on the website, and as sent to prospective exchange students in January-February after your initial application for exchange, as advised for academic year 2024 by USYD, copied 10/11/2024), see below links.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The low rating above should primarily be taken as a reflection on the toil and anguish with which I had to acquire courses. 
A rating of approximately 9 might otherwise have been given as the courses for which I toiled ended up being decent and I otherwise had a thoroughly pleasant time. Having made mates from around the world that I've met on multiple occasions since, and will continue to do so thrice more before the end of 2023.
The city is awesome with great opportunities for exploration “til lands, til vand og i luften” with the mountains to the north (90 min), west (120 min) and south (70 min) away, the sea 30 min to the east, and the harbour going through the city.
Sydney is massive, and different neighbourhoods have different plannings and different concentrations of expat populations such that you get new types of restaurants, bars, decorations and atmospheres in different areas giving you many things to explore.
The nightlife is a bit dry, with most places closing very early and everything, especially alcohol, being very expensive.
The city has decent S-Bahn - style public transport, though this is limited during later hours, inhibiting nightlife possibilities further. Cycling is possible, but rarely are dedicated or protected bike lanes available. You should thus be careful especially for the first month when you're getting used to the paradigm of driving on the left side of the road, and in particular all the unexpected ways cars, trams or other bikes could hit you when they don't travel in the way you expect them to.
Australia has endless possibilities for travel and exploration, near and far, whether you want cold, hot, low or high, cities or vast empty landscapes. I managed to travel thrice during my exchange:
1. I spent the month previous to the start of the semester travelling via Istanbul (half day transfer), Singapore (6 days), Darwin (5 days), Cairns (9 days) and Sydney (14 days). 
2. I did an eight day road trip during spring vacation with three of my mates to Hervey Bay and back. (Travelling the east coast is very popular)
3. Travelled for six weeks after my exchange semester, in which I took two SCUBA diving certificates in Sydney (5 days), road tripped (four days) to Melbourne via Canberra and Kościuszko NP in a relocation campervan (awesome, basically free way to rent a car/van in Oz), explored Melbourne (6 days), walked the OLT in Tasmania and saw Hobart (7+3 days), took another relocation vehicle from Melbourne to Adelaide via the Great Ocean Road and the Grampians (3 days), spent Christmas in Adelaide (5 days) before I flew home via Perth after (10 days of) exploring the nearby areas, taking Quokka selfies, going on tours, base jumping, as well as kayaking and snorkelling in perfect turquoise waters.
My mates mostly chose to travel northwards to QLD or to travel to “nearby” destinations such as Fiji, New Zealand, Bali, Jakarta, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Hawaii and Taiwan.
Travelling to and from Australia is a far way and may involve many stops and airlines. Be sure to check visa and baggage-size and weight -requirements for each hop.  
When travelling Australia, note that the vastness of the country, even near the largest cities and for the closest attractions, require access to a car (!), a willingness to spend >600 DKK / day going on guided tours, or great enthusiasm and ability to cycle. 
There's some online debate as to whether an international or English-languaged-driver's-permit is necessary for EU-permits. To rid yourself of having to worry about possibly finding out the hard way, consider getting an international driver's permit while you are still in Denmark. They cost very little here, but take a couple of weeks to be made, if you think you might want to drive. Alternatively you can get official translations (50 AUD at the Danish Consulate General in Sydney) of any non-English-languaged driver's licence at most consulates (there's Danish representation in the larger Australian cities though you'd have to look up whether they are seasonal)
If you are going to have mates or your family visit you doing your exchange, have them get an international licence as well, if they plan on travelling in Australia. Also have them apply for their tourist visa months (!!!) before their travels, as the tourism visa occasionally takes a long time to process.
Consider that weather in Oz can be intense, and that seasons  (which are not uniform across the country) should be more heavily considered when planning travel - especially if you are similarly inflicted with a predisposition against high temperatures as is the typical Dane.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Main difficulty for me was getting courses sorted. An official USYD international study abroad adviser will be designated, and they will send you info leading up to and during the intro week of your exchange. There's a couple of opportunities to ask academic questions when you arrive, but the answer to any academic question will have its conclusion long been foretold. Non-academic questions can be asked before and after your arrival at the regular USYD student services. Most attempts to enquire with them about academic matters will lead to a deferral to your international study adviser for academic questions. Your international study abroad adviser will be very overworked, only answers by mail, and may at times take over three weeks to respond.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There is an intro week. They show you around campus and arrange some games as well as a couple of tours of, and activities in -the city. You should have all your courses cleared with USYD before you arrive, and preferably way before you arrive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: If you go, call USYD student services before arrival to Australia (for example via Skype) to get your USYD email and access to Canvas set up.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Housing in Sydney is very and increasingly expensive and competitive. Even more so, after lifting of covid restrictions throughout 2022. I lived in a share-house (very common way of getting housing) at 108A Derwent St in Glebe, 700 meters from uni.
The location was perfect, being close to restaurants, shopping, views and the university, but was, as with most share-house accommodation, of terrible quality. 108A Derwent st had mould in the rooms, the toilets as well as common areas, no insulation, and visits by cockroaches as well as rats. I paid 275 AUD / week (~5600 DKK/month) for a 16m^2 room while living with four flatmates (each in separate rooms). When I moved out in November 2022 the price of the room was raised for the next occupants to 350 AUD / week (7200 DKK/month) and was reserved within the first hour of showing the room.
Non-university accommodation is acquired through the likes of
flatmates.com.au
or various facebook groups. Be aware of scammers - do not send any money to reserve private accommodation if you are still in Denmark. You will HAVE TO, (and you should) physically attend a viewing of accommodation, so arrive in Sydney at least two weeks in advance of your semester starting, and attend many viewings to get a sense of the market and the standard of available housing.
I strongly recommend (my #2 top recommendation from my exchange, surpassed only by #1 that you do not attend USYD if you are MSc Statistics or MSc Mathematics) that you book a stay at a hostel in the time until you find permanent accommodation (strongly recommend Mad Monkey's in Kings Cross), to get to meet mates and figure out permanent living situation!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: See above.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
As mentioned at the start, I had a terrible time getting courses approved by USYD (UCPH-side was no problem). 
So: DO NOT(!!) GO ON EXCHANGE TO USYD AS AN ACTUARIAL, STATISTICS OR PURE MATHS STUDENT AT MASTER's LEVEL UNLESS YOU ARE LOOKING FOR A SEMESTER TAKING LOW-LEVEL OR SUBJECT-IRRELEVANT COURSES, OR ARE DEEPLY KEEN ON EMULATING SISYPHOS IN SIGNING UP FOR PROPER ONES. 
To this day I continue to believe that the only reason I got approved for my courses was: 1.  Because I persisted in mailing and calling lecturers, advisors, research institutes, and faculties for months. I went around official signup procedures in order to have my case heard and the objections to me getting the courses I wanted ridiculed by as many non-exchange-study-advisors as possible. 
2. That I, with less than two months until my flight to Australia, wrote my USYD adviser that I was quitting my exchange if they didn't give me proper statistics or data science courses within a certain date.
 If you are wanting to go to Australia, many alternative universities are available for exchange. I considered, and should have chosen either, UniMelb and UNSW.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: As above.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can try USYD student services which have a number you can call from overseas. Many questions will however be deferred to your study abroad adviser, who is very overworked, only answers by mail, often provides responses that lead to more questions than answers and may at times take over three weeks to answer.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As above

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Apply to alternative universities, reduce your expectations for courses, or be prepared to battle everyone to get the courses you want.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The courses I ended up attending were very decent. I attended COMP5048: Visual Analytics, COMP5318: Machine Learning and Data Mining, DATA5441: Networks and High-Dimensional Inference as well as STAT5003: Computational Statistical Methods. 
All courses required substantially less mathematical and statistical maturity than UCPH courses, and could be considered lower than or comparable to (the old 15 ECTS) MatStat. Focus was increasingly on getting to learn methods, concepts and motivation for the methods and concepts (how to implement, and what's the idea behind PCA, Gaussian Mixture models, …) rather than the abstract derivation of their results as is often done at the UCPH Maths institute.
 All courses were attended by non-maths or stats people, with DATA5441 and COMP5318 requiring minimal python skills (for example as acquired in UCPH's NumIntro or via a couple of online courses) and COMP5048 and STAT5003 requiring no prior experience. 
While the courses (except for DATA5441) were relatively shallow, you got to learn about and understand a lot of concepts and methods, the idea behind them, as well as how to work with them in python or R. I fervently believe that UCPH maths should copy STAT5003 and make it obligatory for the BSc specialisation in stats somewhere between Matstat and Reg. This as one is never really taught enough R programming to be self-starting or acquiring some degree of autonomy and ability to use various tools.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: See above. Note you cannot take post-graduate units as a BSc student. To this day I still haven't received an answer regarding whether fourth-years could take postgraduate units.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Attending during semester 2 of 2022, we had hybrid education due to continued covid fears. There is an increased focus on continued assessment via quizzes, weekly or multiple assignments, or projects. As such, you should expect a decent amount of work during the semester as well. As compensation, my final exams in each course only accounted for 40%, 60%, 0% and 33% of the final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
COMP5048: Visual Analytics, 
COMP5318: Machine Learning and Data Mining, 
DATA5441: Networks and High-Dimensional Inference,
STAT5003: Computational Statistical Methods.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Don't go to USYD if you are MSc Mathematics and especially MSc Statistics if you cannot see yourself studying a combination of four of the units present in the lists linked to above. 
The above lists of units are updated for the academic year 2024, and I see no sign that you'd be able to attend the STAT or DATA units I did, lest you desire to endure a months-long, attritional battle of calls and mails. You could choose to do QBUS (Quantitative BUSiness) units, but these are sort of the ‘wrong way around' being targeted at business students that want to do quantitative stuff, instead of quantitative students that want to do business. 
You might be able to sign up for the COMP units above. Maybe especially if you have a Computer Science background or significant number of units therein. I was able to appeal my failed applications to attend *any, including introductory first year* COMP units by circumventing the official registration process and mailing the course-coordinators, lecturers and computer science institute, getting their approval, and then forwarding this to my USYD international study adviser via the ‘regular' USYD student services to exert maximal pressure and get the slightest consideration for my case beyond declaring that computer science units are off-limits to anyone not studying computer science, no matter the level or content of the course, or abilities of the exchange student.
Had I done the exchange again, I'd have changed COMP5048 for COMP5328: Advanced Machine Learning, as STAT5003 and COMP5318 shared a decent bit of their curriculum (though taught so as to be implemented in R and python respectively) and COMP5048, while teaching some ideas of how to work with graphics and interactive graphics in particular, was not really material you couldn't learn elsewhere as well.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Airfares cost approximately 8000 DKK each way. I left my rental contract ten days prior to the agreed upon date, and the rental company charged me a week's rent of 275 AUD for ending the contract early, no matter that they had someone in the next day.
A mate of mine got a 130 AUD = ~ 650 DKK ticket during their spring road trip for going 68 kph in a 60 kph zone.
For insurance, I paid 2860 DKK for IDA's travel insurance made for exchange stays, and 348 AUD = ~ 1750 DKK for the USYD-obligatory Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) which I bought from CBHS.
I got covid in Singapore on my way to Australia resulting in 5k DKK extra cost that was taken care of upon my return by the above travel insurance.
JetStar temporarily mislocated my checked baggage when travelling between Cairns and Sydney, resulting in be having to buy 700 DKK worth of basics. This was covered almost immediately by my travel insurance.
The high personal spending above is an estimate, but mainly reflects the fact that I went travelling for a total of 12 weeks during my exchange.
I spent very little on public transport as I lived within walking distance to uni.
I paid 10 AUD / month for basic phone services.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
You'd think Copenhagen to be more expensive than Sydney. As with all things in Australia, it was the other way around.
The price of food when I went in July 2022 - January 2023 could be considered comparable to if you in Denmark were to always go shopping for organics in Irma or Meny in Hellerup. I only found coconut-milk, pre-made curries from ALDI, haircuts, and domestic biscuits on discount to be less expensive.
Price of accommodation was comparable to private market rates for rooms in shared flats in Copenhagen when I arrived, but became massively more expensive when I left. 
Alcohol is massively more expensive than in DK at all but a few pubs, and in all supermarkets. 
Public transport in Sydney is comparable to that of Copenhagen, (but basically free on Sundays).
Renting automobiles is rather expensive as compared to classical European vacation destinations at 120 AUD / day, which makes the option to do relocation drives a lot more desirable if it fits. 
There's no true Australian equivalent to European budget airlines, which makes air travel within Australia rather expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Unlike at UCPH you don't really socialise with your subject-mates, because everything social at the university is done via various clubs. There exists a wide selection of clubs through the University of Sydney Student Union (USU) that you can look up at their website. I engaged only with the ‘Bushwalkers', as I mostly socialised with the people I'd met at the Mad Monkey's Kings Cross hostel, at the beginning of my stay.
Unlike for example the maths-canteen at HCØ where you can both study and socialise, the campus at USYD is mainly for studying, and is thus often surprisingly sombre and deprived of spirit.
You should also consider signing up for SURF CAMP.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Some events are organised for exchange students by the university study abroad team. For those you'll have to sign up quickly. Lots of opportunities via the clubs, see USU website and above.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: As above, there are lots of clubs that you can engage with, and lots of things to go explore in the city and nearby.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See above. You could easily make a weekend out of going to Canberra or Newcastle, or an extended weekend out of visiting Melbourne. Alternatives closer to Sydney include the Blue Mountains, Royal, Ku-ring-gai-Chase and Sydney Harbour National parks, Manly and shelly beach, go to palm beach, Bondi beach, Bondi to Coogee walk, explore the CBD, go explore West Sydney's neighbourhoods and food (for example on the T2 or T3 to Cabramatta, Parramatta or Liverpool), try Sydney's secret bars or the many gaybars on Oxford Street, go to Kings Cross or the posh east and north east Sydney neighbourhoods such as Rose Bay, Vaucluse and Mosman. Note that ferry transport is excellent and can take you to many different places within the harbour.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: No problems at all. There is a lot of internationals.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Australians are a difficult breed to socialise with at uni lest you engage in clubs, as there is no natural or canonical social activity on campus. Most exchange students group together with other exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing of note. A decent portion of the international students have lower confidence in their English than what I've typically perceived at UCPH.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Australians subscribe to the British pub-concept, which I appreciated a lot as opposed to the more thunderous bar-concept that we typically go with in Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Go to alternative universities than USYD if you are MSc Statistics or similar (check the lists). Make sure whichever uni you exchange to, that the approval for courses at your host institution is solid and settled before you arrive. Make sure that you know what the content, programming languages, degree of abstraction of each course is, prior to your arrival, and that these are satisfactory to you in terms of prerequisites and interest.

2. If you go on exchange, arrive at your destination at least two weeks early, to get to meet people. For example by staying at a hostel. Exchange students typically group together, and the groups typically solidify very quickly. Once the semester starts, they will suddenly be blocking off 30, 40, 50 hours a week on studying that was free to explore the city and socialise previous to the start of the semester.

3. Exchange is often romanticised. Consider that most stays, even the ones that do not go as wrong as mine, will involve a non-insignificant amount of multi level planning and coordination, and is often a significant undertaking both prior to and during the stay.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is possible to attend USYD as a Math Econ student if you are willing and allowed to take ECON units, of which there are plenty (see above link), or if you are going during your BSc

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
1. Getting to meet new people
2. Getting to live and travel new places
3. Getting to contrast your regular life with an alternative one in a very natural and safe environment

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting approval for units commensurate to my academic maturity as a fifth year statistics student.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Nah.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
